script.opening: “Hi, thanks for calling. I’ve got a coil fitting booked for next week but the receptionist said I should talk to a doctor first about which one. I don’t really want hormones if I can avoid it. I just want something I don’t have to think about.”

facts.text: “My son is seven months. I’m still breastfeeding morning and night and once overnight.”
“I’ve been on the mini pill, desogestrel, since my six-week check. I take it every day — I haven’t missed any.”

“They came back two months ago. They’re heavier than before — I’m changing a super tampon every two hours on the first two days, and I’ve flooded through once. Seven days long. Not much pain.” No bleeding between periods or after sex. No pelvic pain or discharge.
“When I was 22 the combined pill made me really low and weepy. I stopped it and was fine. I don’t want to feel like that again.” Mood now is good; no postnatal depression.
No migraines, no clots, no heart problems, no breast cancer, not anaemic as far as she knows, BP fine at the postnatal check. No allergies. “Two babies, both normal deliveries.”
“I’ve been with my husband, Arjun, for ten years. No one else.” Chlamydia test in pregnancy was negative. No symptoms of infection.
“We think two is enough, but I’m not ready for anything permanent.”

If asked how she feels about the fitting, or about previous examinations, or about her births: quietly, “I had a bad tear with my son — a third-degree. The examination at my six-week check was awful, I was shaking. I’m really scared about the fitting. What if I can’t cope and they just carry on?”
“Does the copper one make periods worse?” “Is it safe while breastfeeding?” “Does it hurt?” “Can it go through the womb?”

Friendly and organised; you are a teacher and like clear information. Hold back the fear of the fitting unless the doctor asks how you feel about the procedure, previous examinations or the birth. Once disclosed, become emotional. If the doctor offers adjustments (stop any time, longer slot, female clinician, local anaesthetic, positioning), feel reassured. If the doctor simply says “it’s quick and most people are fine”, say “okay” but sound unconvinced. If the LNG-IUS is explained honestly (local hormone, lighter periods, mood effects possible but less likely), you are open to it; make a decision only after you have heard both.

ice.ideas: A coil is easy, long-lasting contraception; the copper one avoids hormones.
ice.concerns: Feeling low on hormones again; pain and loss of control at the fitting after her traumatic birth; heavy periods getting worse.
ice.expectations: A clear comparison so she can choose, and to know what will happen at the fitting.

cues: “I just want something I don’t have to think about” — wants reliability.
“They’re heavier than before” — the copper IUD may worsen this.
Hesitation when the fitting appointment is mentioned: “Yes… next Thursday.”

checkpoints.text: Takes a contraceptive and medical history relevant to UKMEC — postpartum interval, breastfeeding, current method and adherence, periods (heavy bleeding), mood history, VTE, cancer, cardiovascular risk
Assesses STI risk and pregnancy risk before fitting (consistent desogestrel use) and screens for intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding and pelvic infection symptoms
Explores feelings about the procedure and previous examinations, and elicits the traumatic birth and fear of fitting
Compares copper IUD and LNG-IUS accurately — effect on periods, hormone levels and side effects, duration, when each becomes effective — noting both are UKMEC 1 when breastfeeding beyond 4 weeks
Explains risks with numbers — perforation (higher when breastfeeding), expulsion, infection, ectopic if pregnancy occurs — and what symptoms to report
Plans the fitting with trauma-informed adjustments and pain relief, advises continuing desogestrel until the device is effective, and arranges follow-up (thread self-check, heavy bleeding review)
Responds empathically to the disclosure and makes clear she can stop the procedure at any time
Supports a shared decision, respecting her wish to avoid hormones while giving balanced information

worked.txt: “What matters most to you in a contraceptive?”
“You mentioned heavier periods — the copper coil can make periods heavier and longer, while the hormonal coil usually makes them much lighter.”

“The hormonal coil releases a small amount of progestogen, mostly in the womb, so blood levels are much lower than with the pill. Some people still notice mood changes, but it’s less common — and you could have it removed if you did.”
“About 1 or 2 in 1000 coils go through the wall of the womb when fitted — a bit more likely while breastfeeding. About 1 in 20 come out by themselves, usually in the first year.”
“How are you feeling about the fitting itself?”
“You are in charge. You can say stop at any point and we stop. We can book a longer appointment, use local anaesthetic, and you can bring someone with you.”

f.learning: Pre-fit counselling for intrauterine contraception covers the woman’s priorities, UKMEC eligibility, a comparison of devices, risks with numbers, STI and pregnancy risk, and the fitting itself. Both the copper IUD and the 52 mg LNG-IUS are UKMEC 1 from 4 weeks postpartum, including while breastfeeding. The copper IUD is hormone-free, effective immediately, lasts up to 10 years, and can make periods heavier and more painful; the LNG-IUS usually reduces bleeding (first-line for heavy menstrual bleeding), needs 7 days of additional cover unless fitted early in the cycle (or continue the current method), and the 52 mg device is licensed for contraception for up to 8 years. Risks: perforation about 1–2 per 1000 insertions, about six times higher when breastfeeding; expulsion about 1 in 20; pelvic infection is uncommon and mostly in the first 20 days. Ask about previous examinations and birth trauma: trauma-informed adjustments and the explicit right to stop make fitting safer and more acceptable.

wordPics.clearPass: Elicits priorities and a UKMEC-relevant history, notices the heavier periods and links them to the device choice, uncovers the traumatic birth and fear of fitting and responds with concrete trauma-informed adjustments, explains both devices and their risks with accurate numbers, and reaches a genuinely shared decision with a clear plan for bridging cover and follow-up.
wordPics.pass: Accurate comparison and risks, with a reasonable plan; the fear of fitting is addressed but with fewer practical adjustments, or the link between heavy periods and device choice is less explicit.
wordPics.fail: Gives the copper IUD as requested without discussing her heavy periods, or gives risks without numbers; does not explore feelings about the procedure.
wordPics.clearFail: Inaccurate eligibility advice (for example that coils cannot be fitted while breastfeeding), no risk discussion, or dismissive of her fear (“it only takes a minute”).

avoid.dont: “It only takes a minute — you’ll be fine.”
avoid.instead: “How are you feeling about the fitting? Some people find examinations hard, especially after a difficult birth.”
avoid.why: Minimising pain silences fear and undermines consent.

avoid.instead: “It releases a small amount of hormone, mainly into the womb, so blood levels are much lower than the pill.”
avoid.why: Overstating to persuade is not informed consent.

avoid.instead: “About 1 or 2 in every 1000 — slightly more while breastfeeding.”

model.text: Hello Priya, it’s Dr Mensah. I understand you’re booked for a coil next week and wanted to talk about which one. What matters most to you?
Something I don’t have to think about, and no hormones if possible — the pill made me low years ago.
That’s helpful. How old is your baby, are you breastfeeding, and how are you getting on with the mini pill?
Seven months, still breastfeeding, and I take the desogestrel every day.
Have your periods come back, and what are they like? Any bleeding between periods or after sex, pain or discharge?
Two months ago. Heavier than before — I flooded once. Nothing between.
Any history of clots, migraines, heart problems or breast cancer? And any chance of infection — any new partners?
None of those. Same partner for ten years.
And how are you feeling about the fitting itself?
(quiet) I had a third-degree tear with my son. The check at six weeks was awful — I was shaking. I’m scared I won’t cope and they’ll just carry on.

Thank you for telling me — that sounds really frightening, and it’s completely understandable to feel that way. You will be in control: if you say stop, we stop. We can book a longer appointment with a clinician you choose, use local anaesthetic, try a different position, and you can bring someone with you.

Both coils are safe while breastfeeding at your stage. The copper coil has no hormones, works straight away and lasts up to 10 years, but it often makes periods heavier and more painful — which matters, as yours are already heavier. The hormonal coil releases a small amount of progestogen mostly into the womb; periods usually become much lighter, and it lasts up to 8 years for contraception. Mood changes can happen but are less common than with the pill.
model.why: Balanced comparison tailored to her heavy periods and mood history

model.text: Can it go through the womb? Is that more likely because I’m breastfeeding?

It’s rare — about 1 to 2 in every 1000 fittings — and a bit more likely while breastfeeding, so the nurse takes extra care. About 1 in 20 coils come out on their own, usually in the first year. Infection is uncommon and most likely in the first three weeks. If you did get pregnant with a coil, there’s a higher chance it would be ectopic, so a positive test needs checking quickly.
I think the hormonal one makes sense with my periods. If I feel low I can have it out?

Yes, at any time. Keep taking your desogestrel until the fitting and for 7 days after. Take ibuprofen an hour before. Afterwards, check your threads after each period, and contact us for heavy pain, fever, unusual discharge, or if you can’t feel the threads. I’ll move your appointment to a 40-minute slot and note your preferences so you don’t have to explain again. Does that sound right?
model.why: Bridging cover, pain relief, follow-up and adjustments documented

model.text: Yes. I feel much better about it.

knowledge.guideline: CoSRH UK Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use (UKMEC 2025) · CoSRH (FSRH) Clinical Guideline: Intrauterine Contraception (2023) · CoSRH Contraception after Pregnancy (2017, amended) · NICE NG88 Heavy menstrual bleeding (2018, updated 2021)
knowledge.summary: Both the copper IUD and the 52 mg LNG-IUS are highly effective long-acting methods suitable from 4 weeks postpartum, including during breastfeeding. Choose with the woman according to bleeding pattern, hormone preference and duration; explain risks with numbers; plan a trauma-informed fitting.

points.t: From 4 weeks postpartum, both IUDs are UKMEC 1, including while breastfeeding (between 48 hours and 4 weeks: UKMEC 3). Check for current pelvic infection, unexplained bleeding and pregnancy risk.
Hormone-free; effective immediately; up to 10 years (some devices); also the most effective emergency contraception. May increase menstrual bleeding and pain.

Mainly local action; reduces bleeding and is first-line for heavy menstrual bleeding; licensed for contraception up to 8 years (Mirena) and 5 years for heavy bleeding or HRT. Irregular bleeding is common in the first 3–6 months. Needs 7 days of extra cover unless fitted in the first 7 days of the cycle or the current method is continued.

Perforation up to about 2 per 1000 insertions, about six times higher when breastfeeding and in the first 36 weeks after delivery. Expulsion around 1 in 20, most often in the first year. Pelvic infection uncommon, mostly in the first 20 days. If pregnancy occurs, a higher proportion are ectopic.
Test before fitting if at risk (for example under 25, new or multiple partners). Fitting need not be delayed for results in asymptomatic women.

Offer analgesia (NSAID beforehand, local anaesthetic options); explain each step; a trained assistant; the patient can stop at any time. Trauma-informed care: ask about previous experiences, adapt positioning and pace, offer a chosen clinician and longer slot.
Thread checks; seek help for pain, fever, abnormal discharge, missing threads or a positive pregnancy test.
Mood changes are reported with hormonal methods; the LNG-IUS has low systemic levels. Discuss honestly and agree review.

social.t: A working mother with a baby and a toddler: plan the appointment around childcare and feeds.

legal.t: Informed consent requires discussion of material risks (Montgomery 2015). Consent can be withdrawn at any time during the procedure.

professional.t: GMC decision-making and consent (2020): find out what matters to the patient and support their choice. Record adjustments so she does not have to retell her story.

community.t: NHS contraception guide; Sexwise (coil leaflets); MASIC Foundation for women after obstetric anal sphincter injury.

redFlags: Pelvic pain, discharge or fever (possible infection)
ice: Concern: low mood; pain and loss of control at fitting; heavy periods
Expectation: clear comparison, what happens at fitting

playbook.diagnosis: Woman 7 months postpartum, breastfeeding, seeking IUC; both devices UKMEC 1; heavier periods favour the LNG-IUS; significant procedural anxiety after obstetric trauma.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Both coils are safe for you now. The copper one has no hormones but can make periods heavier; the hormonal one usually makes periods lighter and only releases a tiny amount of hormone.”

management.reflectIce: “You wanted no hormones because of how the pill made you feel — that’s really important. Because your periods are heavier, the hormonal coil might suit you, but it’s your choice.”
management.psychosocial: Longer slot, chosen clinician, stop at any time, local anaesthetic, support person.
sharedPlan: Device chosen by her after balanced information
Continue desogestrel until fitting and for 7 days after (LNG-IUS)
safetyNet: Pain, fever, discharge, missing threads, positive pregnancy test → contact promptly
Review bleeding and mood at 6–12 weeks

pitfalls.intro: A routine counselling call that hides a frightened woman. Candidates who only compare devices miss half the marks.

items.fail: Never asking how she feels about the fitting.
items.why: The previous abandoned examination is in the notes; distress affects consent and safety.
items.fix: Ask about previous examinations and the birth.

items.fail: Fitting the copper IUD as requested without linking it to her heavier periods.
items.why: Likely to worsen her bleeding and lead to removal.
items.fix: Discuss bleeding effects of each device.

items.fail: Risks without numbers, or omitting breastfeeding-related perforation risk.
items.why: Material risks must be explained for consent.

items.fail: Persuading her towards hormones by minimising them.
items.fix: Explain honestly and let her decide.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options

Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Follows “something I don’t have to think about”, “they’re heavier than before” and the hesitation when the fitting appointment is mentioned.
Idea (copper coil avoids hormones); concern (low mood, pain and loss of control at fitting after a traumatic birth, heavier periods); expectation (clear comparison, what fitting involves).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — Feeling low on hormones again; pain and loss of control at the fitting after her traumatic birth; heavy periods getting worse — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.
